No network, no installs, no other input. CPU 1, memory 1GB, 60 seconds. Print one compact JSON object under 9000 characters. Use the observed profile to choose sensible missing/sentinel handling; report sample counts, descriptive effect sizes and limitations. Distinguish association from causality. Check actual indicator labels, never substitute a different outcome silently. No benchmark answers available. Return code without markdown in the code field; conclusion and limitations describe the planned analysis, not invented results. Do not call tools yourself.

dataset.description: This is the panel data created based on the information provided in the paper. The dataset contains information of two groups of countries- Sub-Saharan Africa and Lower Middle Income Countries (LMC) from 1975 to 2015, sourced from the World Development Indicators (WDI) database. It focuses on the relationship between government expenditure on education (% of total expenditure) and per capita GDP (in 2010 US$), using variables like total labor force, gross primary and secondary enrollment, and exports (annual % growth) as key indicators.

response.conclusion: The program will verify indicator labels and report group-specific sample counts, descriptive associations, and annual-change regressions with HAC uncertainty. The supplied profile identifies GNI rather than GDP, so GNI results will be explicitly secondary and the GDP impact question will remain unresolved.
limitations: No analysis results have been computed here.
The profile verifies execution only, not scientific conclusions.
Education expenditure as a percentage of GNI differs from the government-budget spending measure described in the question.
Aggregate observational associations cannot establish causality; the two country groups may overlap.

dataset.description: This is the panel data created based on the information provided in the paper. The dataset contains information of two groups of countries- Sub-Saharan Africa and Lower Middle Income Countries (LMC) from 1975 to 2015, sourced from the World Development Indicators (WDI) database. It focuses on the relationship between government expenditure on education (% of total expenditure) and per capita GDP (in 2010 US$), using variables like total labor force, gross primary and secondary enrollment, and exports (annual % growth) as key indicators.
dataset.name: worldbank_education_gdp.csv

payload.question: In what regions does increased education spending positively impact per capita GDP?

response.conclusion: The supplied results cannot identify any region where increased education spending positively impacts per capita GDP: the recorded outcome is GNI per capita in constant 2015 US dollars, and the observational analysis cannot establish causality. The profile contains 12 indicator-group rows covering two groups and six indicators over 1975–2015 (evidence root: 0ba3f0ddd27dc64f07c7d1ed509c4e262276c83b385611bca633c9a8ecd57029). As a secondary GNI finding, lower-middle-income countries show a positive contemporaneous association between annual changes in education expenditure/GNI share and GNI per capita growth: slope 2.185514 growth units (100 × log points) per percentage-point increase in the share, 95% HAC CI [0.165322, 4.205707], p=0.034728, n=40 annual changes during 1976–2015, R²=0.036414. This positive result is specification-sensitive: the prior-year-change slope is −1.090508 (95% CI [−3.135675, 0.954660]), while the trend-adjusted level slope is negative, −20.018225 (95% CI [−32.350827, −7.685624]), in different level-model units. Sub-Saharan Africa has only five GNI observations, 2011–2015, and four annual changes; its regression associations were not estimable under the recorded analysis criteria. These findings leave the GDP question unresolved (analysis evidence root: 4764eebb61209a68984b3430372a852513e34f220f24771c6b7bf544fdf5a0ff).
limitations: Both recorded executions succeeded with empty stderr. Validator verification covers identity, input hash and execution receipts only; scientific validity is explicitly unverified.
The actual outcome NY.GNP.PCAP.KD is GNI per capita in constant 2015 US dollars, rather than the GDP per capita in 2010 US dollars described in the task.

The exposure NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS measures education expenditure as a percentage of GNI, rather than a percentage of total government expenditure or an absolute spending amount. Share increases need not mean spending increases; the GNI denominator can induce associations.

Lower-middle-income education and GNI series each contain 41 observations. Sub-Saharan Africa has 36 missing GNI years; its education series is complete. Missing values were not interpolated, and models used their longest contiguous complete annual runs. Insufficient data do not establish an absent effect.

The groups may overlap: Sub-Saharan Africa is a geographic aggregate, whereas lower middle income is an income classification. These are not independent country samples, and no formal between-group difference is established.

Reverse causality, omitted factors, trends, structural changes and changing group composition remain possible. Models do not adjust for enrollment, labor participation or exports; HAC intervals use three lags and are pointwise without multiplicity adjustment. Sensitivity models address different relationships and do not support a stable positive causal effect.
